findings.problem: Luke 6:17-49: the included parable is given as Luke 6:39-40. The BSB calls only the blind-leading-the-blind saying a parable (6:39), and 6:40 is a separate saying about a disciple and his teacher. The speck-and-beam lines (6:41-42) that follow could also be read as part of it. The two builders (Luke 6:47-49) is a story-shaped comparison, but it is not listed as included and the text does not call it a parable.
findings.question: Where does an included parable's range end when the text does not mark it: just the verse the BSB calls a parable (6:39), 6:39-40, or 6:39-42? And should Luke 6:47-49 (the two builders) be listed as an included parable even though the text does not call it a parable?

findings.problem: Luke 6:17-49 is typed Sermons, but 6:17-19 is narrative: Jesus comes down, the crowd gathers, and people are healed. The docs say 'Never mix types in one passage' and that a passage breaks wherever the type changes. But they don't say whether a few verses that set the scene go with the sermon they introduce. Splitting them off would leave a 3-verse unit.
findings.question: Can a standalone Sermons passage keep the short narrative setting just before the sermon starts (Luke 6:17-19), or should those verses go to a Narrative passage?

findings.problem: Luke 16:1-13 ends right before 'The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all of this and were scoffing at Jesus' (16:14). Jesus then answers them (16:15-18) and goes on to the rich man and Lazarus (16:19-31). The docs say 'Never split in the middle of a conversation,' but they also say to break at 'a new speaker or speech.' 16:14 is a new audience reacting directly to the teaching just given.
findings.question: Is the break at Luke 16:13/16:14 a natural turn (a new audience), or is it the middle of one conversation, so that 16:14-18 should stay with the shrewd manager?
